title: Initial investigation of progressive structural dysphagia
fairness: Upper endoscopy with directed biopsies is the defensible best offered investigation. Neither passage of liquids nor contrast passage excludes a consequential structural lesion; no confident clinical error identified in the explanation.

Difficulty: progressive solid-food dysphagia already leads to endoscopy before the contrast update is read. The irregular narrowing reinforces the same elementary choice; manometry and premature EUS do not produce two consequential decisions.
Sequence: the initial node is self-contained. Its tissue-before-treatment explanation also rehearses part of the next node's decision.

Review scope: all 18 candidate nodes were reviewed using visible candidate presentation, update, task, option labels and explanations; no separate exhibits are supplied. The 12 historical rewrite rows consolidate into three candidate rewrites. Kept, retired/replaced, parked and held historical records were noted but not re-reviewed. Author self-checks, keys and source claims were not treated as proof. This is an offline editorial review, not source verification or Melissa Rowland's clinical approval; all candidates remain needs_clinician_review. Difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative.
suggestions: Create a genuine diagnostic sequencing problem in which prior examination adequacy or a discordant finding changes which investigation is needed. Supply that information as observations and use credible investigations at the same stage.
If this straightforward initial-endoscopy decision is retained, request explicit acceptance as foundational recognition rather than describing it as a difficult two-step resident item.

title: Suspicious stricture despite negative superficial tissue
clarityIssues: 'Later records show' does not explicitly identify the endoscopy that produced the biopsies and photographs. A short explicit chronology would make the follow-up easier to follow.

cues.phrase: Procedure photographs place the forceps on the smooth proximal lip; the irregular indurated edge lies farther distally.
cues.why: The conspicuously missed target points to the sole sampling option. The alternatives only treat the narrowing, so a reader can choose 'directed lesion biopsies' by matching the narrative problem to its repair.

fairness: Repeat directed sampling is the best offered choice; the negative specimen does not exclude cancer in the unrepresented suspicious lesion. No confident clinical error identified.

The underlying specimen-scope concept is high yield, but the present options collapse it into sampling versus two premature treatments. The forceps-location detail and prior tissue-before-treatment explanation make the answer easy rather than hard.
Sequence is clinically coherent and the update supplies the important findings independently of an earlier correct answer. Prior feedback nevertheless scaffolds the same management rule.
suggestions: Compare credible ways to resolve the remaining diagnostic uncertainty at the same stage, supported by actual prior sampling and lesion observations, instead of two premature stricture treatments.
Keep necessary target and specimen provenance; do not hide inadequate sampling merely to increase difficulty. Make its interpretation change a genuinely competing plan.
Identify the prior procedure directly and keep the preceding explanation from rehearsing this node's full decision.

title: Additional focal biopsy after food-bolus removal

cues.phrase: The irregular mound at the narrowing
cues.why: It repeats 'eccentric nodular mound with an irregular ulcerated surface at the distal narrowing' and is the only independently abnormal lesion offered.
The label itself supplies a benign traumatic explanation, while 'The smooth cardia below the junction' supplies a reassuring description. A nonmedical reader can choose the odd abnormal target.

fairness: Biopsy of the separate suspicious focal lesion is defensible; remote inflammatory samples do not characterize it. The explanation properly distinguishes the two sampling questions.
The completed multilevel sampling does not create a second consequential inference when the other targets are an explicitly traumatic scrape and smooth tissue. This is abnormal-lesion recognition.
Sequence: the later benign focal result and EoE diagnosis can follow this examination coherently. The current retrospective task is complete and does not require later results.
suggestions: Replace normal-tissue and explicitly explained-trauma foils with clinically credible sampling decisions, supplying location and adequacy observations that actually determine the remaining target.
Keep the distinction between remote inflammatory sampling and suspicious focal-lesion sampling, but require interpretation of the record rather than selecting the only abnormal noun phrase.

title: Persistent EoE dysphagia despite inflammatory response
fairness: Continue budesonide and arrange graded dilation is the best offered plan: adequate follow-up histology shows inflammatory control while a fixed nontraversable segment explains continued obstructive symptoms. Re-biopsy and drug escalation are plausible errors in interpreting persistent symptoms.

Two consequential steps survive: distinguish ongoing inflammation from residual fibrostenosis, then choose mechanical treatment while preserving disease control. The known EoE diagnosis is an appropriate management prerequisite, not an answer leak.
No confident clinical error identified in the explanation. 'Only rare eosinophils without active epithelial injury' avoids an invented numerical treatment threshold.

Sequence: focal benign results, multilevel EoE diagnosis and treatment response are explicitly supplied. The node stands with its shared presentation and own update; the preceding biopsy explanation does not disclose the dilation answer.

title: Empiric EoE diet versus sensitization-directed restriction
clarityIssues: The transition from successful budesonide treatment to diet is understandable as a patient choice, but the follow-up plan does not say how medication use will be handled during objective dietary assessment. Avoid implying that dilation itself established disease control.

cues.phrase: Eliminate animal milk for an empiric trial
cues.why: This is the only option framed as an empiric trial; both alternatives explicitly advertise dependence on allergy tests. The answer categories expose the intended rule.

cues.phrase: He wants the least restrictive supported initial trial.
cues.why: 'Initial trial' is echoed only by the milk option. 'Supported' also hints that one option is guideline-concordant rather than presenting a neutral patient preference.

fairness: Empiric milk elimination is defensible among these choices; sensitization without immediate reactions does not establish an EoE trigger. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
This mainly tests recall that IgE/skin testing should not select EoE elimination foods. It does not require two consequential steps; two distractors instantiate the same mistake.
Sequence: the diet decision follows improved swallowing coherently and repeats the relevant EoE context. The prior explanation does not give the milk answer.
suggestions: Use parallel diet labels without embedding 'empiric' versus 'by serum IgE' rationales in the options; keep the test results in the update.

Compare distinct plausible dietary decisions and make an actual treatment or response-assessment issue consequential. If retaining the allergy-testing rule as a single-step item, obtain explicit foundational-purpose acceptance.
Keep objective follow-up in the explanation and clarify the supervised transition from medication to diet without inventing a washout interval.

title: Persistent symptoms after a negative foreign-body radiograph
fairness: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest is the best offered next investigation when persistent symptoms after a possible bone ingestion progress to chest pain, fever and focal tenderness. Direct endoscopy remains a credible distractor for a retained luminal object; repeat films are weaker.

The learner must reject false reassurance from negative radiographs and interpret the new trajectory as possible injury beyond the lumen before selecting the investigation. No key-only wording or diagnosis label supplies that inference.
No confident clinical error identified in the explanation. It describes what CT can establish without declaring the later scan result in advance.
Sequence: the historical hospital setting and sequence are explicit; subsequent CT and retrieval decisions follow coherently. This node stands without later information.

title: Initial removal of an intraluminal sharp esophageal object

cues.phrase: Which initial removal pathway best fit
cues.why: The task presupposes removal and grammatically disadvantages 'Inpatient observation and serial radiographic reassessment' before any clinical reasoning.

cues.phrase: no extraluminal object, gas or collection
cues.why: With the task already selecting removal, this explicit uncomplicated-luminal description leaves the less invasive of only two removal options. The negative findings are clinically useful, but this option set turns them into a simple elimination ladder.

fairness: Emergency therapeutic esophagoscopy is the defensible offered initial route for the represented sharp luminal object. Saliva passage does not justify observation. No confident clinical error identified.
Recognition of a sharp esophageal object followed by urgent endoscopic removal is a high-yield safety rule, but the offered choices do not sustain two consequential steps or moderate/hard difficulty.

Sequence: CT follows the prior imaging decision logically. The update is self-contained for location and complication status; the previous explanation anticipates route selection but does not name this answer.
suggestions: Ask a neutral next-management task if observation remains an option.
Either explicitly seek acceptance as a safety-recognition exception or develop a supported complication/access distinction with genuinely competing extraction plans.
Retain necessary complication observations; do not remove safety information to make the item harder.

title: Failed extraction with extraluminal migration and mediastinal infection

cues.why: This defeats 'retrieval through the esophagus' by ordinary spatial reasoning. Surgery is the only offered plan that directly reaches the stated target.
The distractor 'Repeat flexible endoscopic retrieval through the esophagus' repeats the already failed approach without a changed capability or route, providing a novelty shortcut.

fairness: Thoracic operative retrieval with mediastinal source control is the best offered pathway for the migrated object and infected mediastinal pocket. Covered-stent placement does not retrieve the extraluminal object. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The near-aortic location is consequential and should remain, but the current choices allow a nonmedical reader to select surgery by reach and prior failure. Several dramatic findings do not make this a hard two-step item.

Sequence: failed retrieval and a new CT support a coherent worsening course. The update provides the changed anatomy, infection and started supportive care without requiring recall of the earlier answer.
suggestions: Retain the location and source-control facts, but compare credible next procedural plans at the same stage rather than repeating a failed luminal approach.
If this remains a recognition/escalation item, label and obtain acceptance of that purpose instead of claiming difficult independent reasoning.
Keep any required vascular assessment or operative coordination within clinician-reviewed planning; the text does not establish a particular aortic injury or justify inventing one.

title: Imaging for suspected postendoscopic perforation
clarityIssues: 'Chest CT with esophageal contrast assessment' does not clearly state the intended CT/esophagography protocol; readers may interpret its oral and intravenous contrast components differently.

cues.phrase: records of an esophageal injury during diagnostic endoscopy
cues.why: The shared presentation announces the eventual injury before the initial diagnostic node. It reduces the intended inference from postprocedural symptoms to suspicion of injury.

fairness: CT is a reasonable and often preferred initial investigation, but fluoroscopic contrast esophagram is also a recognized diagnostic route for suspected esophageal perforation. The visible record does not clearly establish why it is inferior in this particular patient.

The explanation supports CT's usefulness but never resolves the closest alternative. This is a potentially nonunique best answer, not a confident claim that CT is clinically wrong. Exact ranking requires clinician/source verification, which was not performed under the no-network instruction.

Potential two-step reasoning is present: overcome the negative radiograph, then choose a study that evaluates the injury and its extent. The unresolved alternative does not count as legitimate difficulty.
Sequence: the later CT result follows naturally; the retrospective presentation itself supplies diagnosis-related hindsight. The node otherwise states a complete historical decision.
suggestions: Use neutral postprocedure follow-up wording in the shared presentation so the initial node does not announce the injury.
Define the intended CT protocol and supply a real, supported patient-specific reason that makes CT better than esophagram, or replace the competing esophagram option.
Have Melissa explicitly adjudicate the CT-versus-esophagram ranking and revise the explanation to address the actual nearest competitor before accepting this version.

title: Initial management of a contained esophageal perforation
clarityIssues: 'Which initial esophageal intervention plan' is awkward when the intended answer is surveillance without an intervention; 'management plan' would include all choices naturally.

cues.why: This extreme option is poorly competitive after the update explicitly supplies a small contained injury, improving physiology, no obstruction and no pre-existing esophageal disease. It functions as padding rather than a credible resident error.

fairness: Closely monitored nonoperative care is defensible for the described early contained injury in a stable patient at an expert unit. The shared antimicrobials, withheld oral intake and nutrition support prevent the surveillance option from meaning neglect.

Two meaningful steps are present: interpret containment/drainage together with physiology, then decide whether immediate closure is required. Primary repair is a plausible competing plan, but resection/diversion is not competitive in this exact scenario.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Suitability for nonoperative care remains a clinician judgment; the explanation appropriately limits rather than universalizes it.

Sequence: the early CT and clinical stabilization follow the imaging node coherently. This update supplies its own management eligibility facts. Later deterioration does not retroactively make this initial choice wrong.
suggestions: Use a neutral management lead-in.
Replace the resection/diversion foil with a credible initial closure strategy after clinician review, and include the observations needed to distinguish it from surveillance.
Preserve containment, physiology, absence of diseased/obstructed esophagus and expert monitoring; these are necessary eligibility facts, not details to delete merely because they favor the answer.

title: Reconstruction after deterioration to a free esophageal leak
fairness: Reinforced primary closure with feeding access is the best offered reconstruction when debridement leaves bleeding healthy edges that approximate without tension. Diversion/resection are competing responses to concern about tissue failure or severe contamination.

The learner must recognize that the new leak changes the need for source control, then assess the actual operative tissue rather than reflexively escalate to resection because observation failed. Healthy approximating edges are necessary operative findings, not inappropriate answer teaching.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The explanation keeps drainage and nutritional support within the operative plan and does not invent a time cutoff that automatically prohibits repair.

Sequence: a contained injury can deteriorate into a free pleural leak; the earlier surveillance answer and this new reconstruction are not contradictory. The current update and task stand alone at exploration, with prior feedback not naming the repair.

title: Caustic injury with full-thickness loss of wall enhancement
fairness: Emergency exploration and removal of nonviable tissue is the best offered pathway for the represented full-thickness nonenhancement on an adequately enhanced study. Waiting for free gas or hypotension would be a consequential error.

The learner must interpret absence of wall enhancement despite adequate vascular enhancement, then act despite reassuring hemodynamics and no free gas. Endoscopic grading and monitored care are credible alternatives for a different depth/viability assessment.
The stem supplies observations rather than the diagnosis 'necrosis'; that term appears only as a treatment implication in the option and in feedback. No strong wording-only shortcut identified.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified, although precise CT interpretation and operative extent require clinician review; the item appropriately avoids dictating a specific resection from the limited record.
Sequence: the initial historical decision is complete. The next post-reconstruction stricture node introduces a different phase and has its own anatomical clarity issue, recorded separately.

title: Dilation approach after caustic injury and reconstruction
clarityIssues: 'After later reconstruction restored alimentary continuity' and 'a separately injured cervical segment' leave the actual conduit, retained esophagus and relation of the stenoses to anastomoses unspecified. This is an important anatomical gap after the preceding necrosis/resection pathway.
The choices overlap in technique: a through-the-scope balloon may also be wire-guided and used with fluoroscopy. 'Under direct vision' does not explicitly exclude that combination.

cues.why: 'Placement of a temporary fully covered esophageal stent' is not a dilation approach. The task removes that distractor without using the anatomy.

fairness: Fluoroscopic wire-guided dilation is defensible for a long, angulated, multiple, nontraversable post-caustic narrowing. The explanation identifies a real safety issue in defining the unseen course.

Potential two-step reasoning is worthwhile: interpret complex anatomy and incomplete endoscopic access, then choose a controlled dilation route. Overlapping option definitions and unclear reconstructed anatomy undermine exact uniqueness.
No confident clinical error is asserted about through-the-scope dilation itself. The problem is that the option labels do not describe mutually exclusive guidance strategies.

Sequence: prior thoracic necrosis followed by a preserved injured cervical segment is possible, but the narrative makes the reader reconstruct too much of the intervening surgery. The later item needs an explicit concise anatomical summary to stand alone.
suggestions: State the reconstruction and where the retained native segment, conduit, anastomosis and strictures lie, using only clinically supported details needed for this decision.
Use a neutral next-procedure task if stenting remains offered, or make all options actual dilation strategies.
Describe mutually exclusive guidance approaches explicitly and have a clinician verify their ranking in the specified reconstructed anatomy; do not invent dilation increments or waiting intervals.

title: Zenker treatment with restricted neck extension and pulmonary risk
fairness: Flexible endoscopic septum division is the best offered approach given symptom-linked pouch emptying, inability to extend the neck and significant prior anesthetic recovery problems. Rigid stapling and open diverticulectomy are real established competitors.

The resident must interpret the functional study as symptomatic pouch disease and apply access/anesthetic constraints to procedure selection. Naming the neck restriction is necessary patient-specific information, not a reason to delete the deciding finding.
No strong nonmedical wording shortcut identified: the labels are comparable procedure names and do not explicitly say which avoids the supplied constraints.

The explanation appropriately says flexible treatment is an established option and leaves actual anesthesia planning to specialists. It does not guarantee avoidance of general anesthesia or universal superiority over open treatment.
Standalone case: the presentation, update and task contain the needed context. High yield is judged for the Zenker/procedure-selection principle, not a claim about official examination frequency.

title: Treatment intent with biopsy-confirmed hepatic metastases

cues.phrase: Systemic anticancer therapy selected through oncology
cues.why: This is the only broadly qualified referral/selection answer beside two specified definitive locoregional treatments. 'Selected through oncology' adds a cautious authority cue rather than naming a comparable treatment strategy.

fairness: Systemic treatment is the defensible offered strategy for multiple biopsy-confirmed hepatic metastases. Technical resectability of the primary does not establish a curative esophagectomy indication. No confident clinical error identified.

The core concept is very high yield, but matching liver carcinoma plus multiple bilateral lesions directly establishes disseminated disease. Applying the elementary metastatic-versus-local treatment rule is not two consequential steps with credible competition here.
The stated activity and technical removability are legitimate temptations for overvaluing resectability, but they do not make the question difficult for the intended resident audience.
Standalone case: completed staging and tissue comparison are explicit. The known primary diagnosis is appropriate for this management task.
suggestions: Make all choices comparable concrete treatment strategies and remove the key-only 'selected through oncology' qualification; do not add an unsourced drug regimen merely to lengthen the key.
Either obtain acceptance of a foundational staging/treatment-intent item or introduce a supported genuinely unresolved staging/management decision whose interpretation changes the plan.
Retain the histologic confirmation if the task assumes metastatic disease; withholding it simply to create doubt would risk unfairness.

title: Residual mucosal neoplasia at a lateral resection margin
clarityIssues: 'Endoscopic re-treatment' leaves the actual intervention unspecified. It could mean repeat resection or ablation, which need not be interchangeable for a visible residual neoplastic focus.

cues.phrase: Endoscopic re-treatment of the residual mucosal focus
cues.why: The key repeats the task's 'residual focus'; 'Endoscopic surveillance of the unresected mucosal focus' advertises leaving that focus untreated. Their framing favors the active option before the pathology is interpreted.

fairness: The intended local-treatment strategy is defensible with intramucosal, well-differentiated disease, clear deep margin and no lymphovascular invasion. A positive lateral edge does not by itself mandate esophagectomy.
Two meaningful steps are present: distinguish local margin incompleteness from histologic regional-risk features, then act on a visible remaining focus. Those findings should remain.

No confident clinical inaccuracy is asserted for the general strategy. Fairness is limited by the generic procedure label and the absence of explicit feasibility if a particular endoscopic resection technique is intended.
Standalone case: pathology orientation and the later visible finding are coherent, and the task can be understood without another node.
suggestions: Name the actual proposed endoscopic treatment for the visible lesion and provide any observation needed to establish that it is feasible.
Use neutral parallel option wording, such as actual resection and surveillance plans, without labeling the surveillance target 'unresected' as a critique.
Keep the explanation's separation of lateral local clearance from deep invasion/regional risk, while matching it to the specific treatment being offered.

title: Additional treatment after locally complete high-risk endoscopic resection
fairness: Referral for esophagectomy with regional lymphadenectomy is the best offered option for a fit patient with deep submucosal invasion and lymphatic involvement after endoscopic local clearance. Clear local margins and nonenlarged nodes do not settle regional disease risk.

The two consequential steps are interpreting pathological risk independently of margin status, then selecting regional treatment despite reassuring staging images. Surveillance is the credible closest error; scar resection is a weaker but distinct local-versus-regional error.
No material nonmedical cue identified. 'Tumor nests lie in endothelial-lined lymphatic spaces' requires clinical interpretation rather than merely repeating the keyed treatment label.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The explanation explicitly limits its ranking to the offered plans and does not claim that every possible chemoradiation strategy is inferior.
Standalone case: local pathology, distant staging and basic operative-fitness context are present. The question is high yield without requiring an invented nodal-risk percentage or depth cutoff.

title: Staged removal of an embedded partially covered esophageal stent
clarityIssues: 'Temporary coaxial fully covered stent placement' does not explicitly say that the second stent is placed within the embedded one as a staged removal strategy. Its relationship to the requested removal task relies on specialist terminology.

cues.phrase: that end cannot be mobilized with the initial gentle grasp
cues.why: This makes immediate traction look like repetition of an already failed maneuver; it weakens that distractor without establishing why a different extraction technique would be appropriate.

cues.phrase: Thoracic esophageal resection and reconstruction for stent removal
cues.why: The only surgical option is disproportionately extensive in a stable case with no leak or migration. Between continued pulling and major resection, the staged endoscopic option becomes the conspicuous middle choice.

fairness: An embedded partially covered stent and a staged stent-in-stent approach are a defensible interpretation and treatment sequence. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in that intended technique.

Two-step reasoning is possible: infer tissue embedding from the device and tissue findings, then select a staged removal technique. The precise method is specialist endoscopic knowledge; unfamiliarity alone should not be labeled hard reasoning.

HighYield is false for this narrow stent-in-stent technique relative to core general-surgery/ABSITE decisions; this is a qualitative scope judgment, not a verified blueprint exclusion. Benign-stricture complications are relevant, but this exact technical rescue is a lower-priority addition.
Standalone case: the stricture, device history and current complication status are supplied. The explanation establishes the staged intent more clearly than the answer label does.
suggestions: Spell out that a fully covered stent is placed within the embedded device for planned staged removal, using comparable specificity across the choices.
Replace the extreme surgical foil with a clinician-vetted competing removal strategy and make the findings actually distinguish the plans.

Consider reserving this as an explicitly advanced endoscopy item or replacing it in the core batch with a more commonly tested benign-stricture decision; do not make technique obscurity the source of difficulty.
